extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators and researchers in mathematics education (real analysis instructors, undergraduate instructors interested in limit instruction)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and criteria for instructional design and analysis when teaching the formal definition of sequence convergence, especially using concrete metaphors (the 'party' metaphor), multiple representational registers, and tasks that reveal dependencies among ε, K, and n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathways to develop formal definition-based reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Three primary pathways have been described for the development of formal definition-based reasoning about limits: (1) exploring a range of examples to develop a definition that uniquely describes them; (2) developing 'generic examples' through graphical explorations; and (3) extracting meaning from the formal definition itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each pathway has benefits and limitations: the examples pathway can be slow and produces variability across students; graphical/generic examples sometimes support and sometimes inhibit movement to formal reasoning (graphical convincing power); extracting meaning directly from the formal definition is another route. Use of these pathways should be chosen with awareness of their trade-offs (Swinyard 2008; Pinto & Tall 2002; Dubinsky et al. 1988).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete metaphor to support transition to formal reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a concrete metaphorical domain (e.g., the 'party' metaphor) to instantiate conditions on the parameters of sequence convergence so students can first form a property-based notion before mapping to the formal definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The party metaphor mapped epsilon neighborhoods to 'places', indices to 'time/people', and K to a cutoff after which 'everyone shows up.' This helped one student (Tidus) develop a property-based conception and facilitated some correct reasoning (e.g., uniqueness of limits, irrelevance of finitely many changes). However, metaphors can introduce false lines of reasoning (e.g., treating epsilon as fixed), so instructors should monitor and guide eventual accommodation to full formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present definitions in multiple linguistic/register representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use and explicitly label multiple linguistic registers for the concept: metaphorical register, intuitive register, and formal-symbolic register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The professor alternated among concrete metaphorical descriptions, an intuitive 'gets closer and closer' statement, and the formal epsilon-K-n symbolic definition. Explicit translation between registers (verbal mapping and board work) supports students' ability to reinterpret the formal definition in accessible terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate informal intuitive definitions into rigorous epsilon-K-n formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage students in iteratively amending an intuitive statement (e.g., 'we can make the terms of the sequence stay as close to L as we wish by going far enough out in the sequence') into a rigorous form: 'given ε>0, there exists K such that for all n ≥ K, xn ∈ (L − ε, L + ε)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Class discussion that asks 'How can we make this more rigorous?' and teacher-led consolidation into formal notation helps students see the concrete meaning of quantifiers and parameter roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize interrelationship and dependence of ε, K, and n
rubrics_metrics.description: Make explicit the roles and dependencies among the parameters ε (neighborhood size), K (cutoff/index), and n (term index), including that K generally depends on the chosen ε and n ranges over indices ≥ K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students must learn that for a different ε there may exist a different K ('for every ε>0 there exists K...'). Activities that focus on this dependence (e.g., asking how K changes with ε) promote correct interpretation of universal/existential quantifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instill arbitrariness/universality of ε (for every ε > 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure students understand that the definition requires the condition to hold for every ε>0 rather than a single fixed epsilon chosen once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tasks and probing questions that require considering multiple ε values simultaneously (e.g., Cauchy sequence arguments, contrasting 'given ε>0' vs 'for every ε>0') so students confront and accommodate the universal quantifier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use graphical number-line and term-enumeration representations judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent sequences with number-line diagrams and term-enumeration visuals to link intuition to formal conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphical representations (number lines, term lists) can help visualize neighborhoods and tails, but can also be overly convincing and inhibit abstraction; instructors should pair graphical work with explicit discussion of its limitations and relation to formal quantifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote property-based (definition-based) reasoning over exemplar-based reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage reasoning founded on definitions and properties (applying to entire classes) rather than relying solely on familiar examples or case-based analogies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight the mathematical community's valuing of property-based reasoning and design tasks that require applying the definition to novel examples so students practice generalization rather than relying on exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating epsilon neighborhoods as fixed 'places' (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discourage conceptualizing epsilon neighborhoods as single static 'places' that cannot vary, since this view limits thinking about multiple epsilons and the universal quantifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper documents a student who viewed neighborhoods as locations or fixed-size buildings, which impeded reasoning about varying epsilon; use contrastive examples that force consideration of different neighborhood sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tasks that demonstrate finite changes don't affect convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Include tasks that alter finitely many initial terms (change first K terms) to show that such modifications do not affect the limit of a sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tasks (true/false items, constructing modified sequences) reinforce the notion of 'tail' behavior and help students grasp why only the eventual terms matter for convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage encapsulation/unitizing of the ε-K-n schema (K-condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Support students in encapsulating the interrelated ε-K-n condition into a compact mental schema (the 'K-condition') so they can reason without continuously coordinating quantifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This encapsulation (unitizing) makes future reasoning more fluent; instructors should scaffold students from explicit coordination to internalized schemas and then check that the universal aspects (for every ε) remain present in the encapsulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage disequilibrium and feedback to prompt accommodation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use internal cognitive conflict (students noticing that their proofs don't match definitions) and external feedback (loss of points, instructor prompts) to motivate students to revise their schemas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design assessments and discussions that reveal mismatches between student concept images and formal definitions so that students experience the need to accommodate and refine their conceptual structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research methods for studying student conceptual development
rubrics_metrics.description: For pedagogical research, gather multiple data sources (field notes, biweekly professor interviews, weekly student interviews, students’ written notes, and exams) and code transcripts using open coding to identify categories of reasoning and changes over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select interview participants to represent a distribution of prior achievement (e.g., students with A, B, C grades), record and transcribe interviews, capture classroom board work and gestures, and iteratively develop interview questions tied to classroom events to probe evolving concept images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select participants to represent a variety of prior achievement
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying conceptual change, include participants across a range of course grades/abilities (e.g., one or two students with A, B, and C in prerequisite courses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sampling helps observe how different prior proficiencies interact with instructional interventions like metaphors and register translation.
